title: Fall vaccines 2026: What to know about flu, Covid and RSV | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

There’s a bit of a chill in the air, pumpkin spice in your coffee and children back to school — which means the threat of respiratory viruses like Covid-19, influenza and RSV is looming.

Some respiratory illnesses have arrived already. Seasonal influenza activity is still low at the national level, data from theUS Centers for Disease Control and Preventionshows.

But certain flu metrics are inching up – especiallyin the West. Health officials in Washington state’s King County note that since mid-August there has been anincrease in people with fluvisiting emergency departments in the area.

Vaccines that help prevent illness and reduce the risk of serious infections and hospitalization are now available, and for some people, this is the right time to roll up their sleeves.

Typically, the CDC launches a fall campaign around this time of year, recommending seasonal immunizations such as the flu shot and Covid-19 vaccines. But after sweeping changes to the agency’s vaccine advisory committee during the second Trump administration and ongoing lawsuits, the CDC recently posted guidance online to follow last year’s recommendations for flu and Covid-19.

Meanwhile, the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’sVaccine Integrity Projectlaunched their ownindependent reviews of this fall’s vaccines– including those forflu,CovidandRSV– which was published in September in the medical journal JAMA.

The review papers helped inform2026-27 respiratory virus immunization recommendationsreleased by several medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

“For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP,” Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a news briefing.

“Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter,” Gellin said.

“Clinicians will still have patients to care for. Parents will still have decisions to make for their children, and older Americans, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions will still need to know how best to protect themselves,” he said. “We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance.”

The US Department of Health and Human Services has not responded to CNN’s request for comment on the groups’ recommendations.

Flu, Covid-19 and RSV immunizations are now available at most major pharmacies.

“And really reassuringly, insurers have indicated to the major groups that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations,” Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in a news briefing.

Ordering through Vaccines for Children, the federal program that provides routine immunizations at no cost to children who are uninsured or underinsured or whose families may not otherwise be able to afford them, has also started. About half of US children are eligible for the program.

“Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives,” Nosal said in a news release. “As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients.”

The groups eligible for RSV immunizations include older adults, pregnant people and infants.

“People age 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75 years old, should get one dose,” Nosal said. “This is not an annual vaccine. If you got one before, you do not need a new one this year. Getting one should protect you throughout the entire season.”

During pregnancy, RSV vaccination is recommended in the third trimester, between weeks 32 and 36.

Children younger than 8 months should be immunized against RSV using a monoclonal antibody unless their mother got an RSV vaccination during pregnancy, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

“If the mother’s immunization status is unknown, that child should be immunized,” Racine said in the briefing. He added that children between 8 months and 19 months of age who are in certain high-risk groups for severe disease are also recommended to get the RSV monoclonal antibody.

And a single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for adults who have weakened immune systems.

“Immunosuppressed individuals are at higher risk for severe disease than immunocompetent individuals,” Dr. Dan Barouch, director of the Center for Virology and Vaccine Research at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, who was not involved in the new recommendations, said in an email. “The vaccines are also generally less effective in immunosuppressed individuals compared with immunocompetent individuals.”

For older adults, RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall.

The advice slightly changed this year for pregnant people.

“ACOG now recommends that pregnant individuals receive a single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, from September 1 through March 1 instead of only through January 31,” Dr. Christina Davidson, chief medical officer of the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, said in the news briefing.

“We made this change because the RSV disease season is now occurring later in the spring, and it is also more severe than it used to be,” Davidson said. “The extension of the eligibility window will help provide pregnant patients and their infants with additional protection.”

For infants, the RSV monoclonal antibody is typically recommended around virus season, from October through March.

Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu shot.

“On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to go to the doctor by 30% to 60%,” Nosal said.

“Adults 65 years and older should get an enhanced flu vaccine, one that is high-dose, adjuvanted or recombinant, when it’s available,” she said. “But do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available.”

And for the first time, anmRNA-based flu vaccineis available for use in adults 50 and older.

The flu vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy, but pregnant people should avoid the nasal spray version, according to the recommendations.

“Pregnant and postpartum people still have a significantly higher risk of developing serious complications from infection compared with non-pregnant people,” Davidson said.

“The inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccines remain the only vaccines that are recommended for use in pregnancy in any trimester, so please work with your OB care clinician or pharmacist to get these,” she said. “Most importantly, if you are able to get the vaccine while you are pregnant, the immunity will also, in part, pass on to your baby.”

October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, Nolan said, because “protection wanes throughout the season.”

Some providers use the slogan “flu before boo” to remind people to get a flu shot before Halloween.

Getting an updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for adults.

“If you’re older than 19, we recommend getting the Covid-19 vaccine,” Nosal said.

“This is especially important for people who are 65 years and older, at increased risk for severe Covid infection and those who’ve never received a Covid-19 vaccine,” she said. “For those adults 65 years and older, they should receive a second dose of the updated Covid-19 vaccine six months after that season’s initial dose to help maintain protection as immunity wanes over time.”

The vaccine is also recommended for infants between 6 months and 23 months of age, and children in certain high-risk groups or those whose families request vaccination.

And for people who are immunocompromised, the annual updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for ages 6 months and older.

Last year, the CDC recommended Covid-19 vaccines based on conversations with the patient’s healthcare provider, known as shared decision-making, Barouch noted, but the agency “also emphasized that the risk-benefit of the vaccines is most favorable for individuals who are at higher risk of severe disease.”

Davidson, of ACOG, said the vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy.

“The most important message is this: If you are pregnant, considering pregnancy or are a new or breastfeeding parent, please get your vaccine or your annual booster. All four of the available Covid vaccines are safe for you,” Davidson said.

Moderna offers two mRNA shots, Pfizer and BioNTech have another, and Sanofi and Novavax offer a more traditional protein-based version.

“A recommendation for the Covid vaccine is based on more than five years of research and millions of administered doses,” Davidson said. “I want to emphasize that the evidence has found no increased risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, small for gestational age birth or birth defects. The risks of complications from Covid for pregnant people and their babies, however, is high. So please get the vaccine.”

It’s recommended to get the updated vaccine now, but if you have been recently infected with Covid, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the vaccine.

The updated Covid-19 vaccine “targets the most recent strain that’s been circulating, and so if you want to update your protection, that’s the best way to do it,” Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, president-elect of the American Medical Association, said in a news briefing.

“You know, your computer constantly needs to be updated. Well, your immune system, your immunity needs to be constantly updated too,” she said. “You’re going to get your most protection in those first few months after the vaccine. So if you have a big event – if you have to go to a wedding, or if you’re going on some fabulous trip, or you’re going to a fabulous birthday party, or just any birthday party or get-together – think about getting that vaccine a couple of weeks before that event, so you’ll stay healthy and well.”
